description: Orbit404 is tackling the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge: an interactive map that ranks landing sites near the Moon's south pole by slope, sunlight, Earth visibility and distance to water-ice craters, using NASA LRO data. Led by a CS Master's student at Universitaet Paderborn. Looking for teammates in Python/geospatial data, web dev (maps/React), ML, or design & video. Fully virtual, English/Hindi. Let's find the best spot on the Moon together!
summary:
Horizon404 is a web app that tells you whether a lander at the Moon's south pole will see the Sun and the Earth, and for how long. Pick any spot on the map and a landing date, and it computes hour by hour how much of the solar disk clears the real terrain skyline, when Earth is in view for direct radio contact, how long the longest night lasts and whether your battery survives it, the local landing slope, and the best landing dates over the next 12 months.

At the pole the Sun barely rises above the horizon, so a ridge 50 km away can switch a lander off. Intuitive Machines' IM-1 landed on a ~12° slope in 2024 and tipped over. The data to avoid this exists (NASA LRO LOLA terrain, JPL ephemerides), but the tools are built for specialists. Horizon404 turns it into answers in three clicks, with maps, a 360° sky view, 3D terrain, an animated light-and-shadow movie of the pole and a year-at-a-glance barcode. Sun and Earth positions match JPL Horizons to 0.00001°.
details:
What it does

Horizon404 answers the questions a lunar mission planner asks first about a south-pole landing site: the share of time with sunlight and Earth in view at the same time (power + comms); when the next sunset, sunrise, Earthset and Earthrise happen, and how long the longest night is compared with the battery; a 360° sky view from the lander with the Sun and Earth paths drawn against the real terrain skyline; the best landing dates over the next 12 months for a 14-day surface mission; landing slope safety (safe below 5°, caution up to 10°, hazard above); and what-if settings for antenna/solar mast height, battery endurance and mission window. A Compare tab puts sites side by side.

How it works

Terrain: NASA LRO LOLA LDEM_75S_120M (120 m elevation model south of 75°S). Skyline: for each site we cast 720 rays out to 200 km and record the highest terrain angle in every direction, including lunar curvature and mast height. Sun and Earth: JPL DE421 ephemeris and NAIF lunar frame kernels (via Skyfield) give their azimuth and elevation every hour in the Moon's mean-Earth frame, libration included. Visibility: the fraction of the solar disk above the skyline gives power; Earth above the skyline gives direct-to-Earth comms. From these we derive windows, nights, best dates and maps. Precomputed suitability maps (3 km grid) and a 0.5 km light-and-shadow movie cover the whole pole region.

Validation

Sun/Earth positions agree with JPL Horizons to 0.00001°. 18 automated tests cover known cases, e.g. Apollo 11 always sees Earth, the exact pole, and slope on flat floors vs crater walls. The map layers were checked against the full per-site calculation.

Examples from the live app

IM-1 Odysseus landing spot: 11.6° slope (hazard); Malapert summit nearby: 1.8°. Lunar day from 14 Nov 2026: Malapert 74% power + comms vs the Shackleton connecting ridge 45% (both have full sun; Earth contact makes the difference). A two-week launch slip (14 → 28 Nov) drops a 14-day mission at the ridge from 78% to 16% power + comms. At the geographic pole, raising the mast from 2 m to 20 m lifts the best 14-day window from 61% to 96%.

Benefits and impact

Mission teams can screen candidate sites and launch dates in seconds before running detailed analyses. Students and the public can see why the south pole is so hard: a Learn tab, guided question chips, a live "now" view and share links make it easy to explore and explain.

Tools

Python (Skyfield, NumPy, FastAPI), TypeScript, React, Vite, Plotly, Three.js; hosted on Vercel. Open source on GitHub: https://github.com/indudhara59/horizon404 · Slides: https://horizon404.vercel.app/demo/

What makes it creative

It shows time as well as place: an animated movie of light and shadow sweeping the pole, a barcode with every hour of a year in one picture, 3D terrain lit by the computed Sun, and a "lander's eye" view from the mast top.

Use of AI

An AI coding assistant helped write and debug parts of the code and draft documentation and slide text. All science inputs are NASA/JPL data, and results were validated against JPL Horizons and automated tests. No SI-generated images, video or audio: the demo video is our own screen recording and voice.
